solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: About to break doddery old president (twice): it's the law, jokingly

indicators.note: one piece breaking another is set inside it, splitting it apart

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for president, written two times
C is short for circa, Latin for about

indicators.note: a doddery person totters about, so these letters wobble into a new order

explanation.surface: A satirical swipe at a tottering elderly president, with a jokey nod to the police.
explanation.walkthrough: C (about) is set 'to break' PP, giving PCP; 'doddery' rearranges OLD into LOD.
explanation.definitionFit: PC Plod is a humorous British name for the police, after the policeman in the Noddy children's books.

clue.text: Stupid advice to overworked Cyclops?

definitions.meaning: the straight sense: lacking any idea
Cyclops is this puzzle's setter; split the answer in two and it becomes a tip on how to cut his workload

explanation.surface: Someone tells the Private Eye setter he's working too hard.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as CLUE LESS, the answer is exactly what you'd tell a setter swamped with clue-writing. The question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for the first sense (without a clue, so dim); the second sense is a whimsical re-reading of the same letters as a two-word instruction.

clue.text: Awful fun to own Scottish jet

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: ain is the Scots form of own

explanation.surface: A grumble that it is no fun to own a Scottish jet aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' rearranges FUN TO into FOUNT. 'Jet' looks like an aircraft but it is a spurt of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A fountain sends up a jet of water, so the two words name the same spray.

clue.text: 'Olde' variations in S&M? Hardly ever

indicators.note: one piece set in another goes inside it

parts.note: the letters S and M taken from the abbreviation

indicators.note: variations on a word play its letters in a different order

explanation.surface: A cheeky aside that olde-worlde variations in sadomasochism hardly ever happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variations' rearranges OLDE into ELDO, which goes 'in' between S and M.
explanation.definitionFit: Seldom is an adverb meaning rarely, the same as hardly ever.

clue.text: Feeling popular court upholds fools

indicators.note: to uphold is to hold up, so in a down entry the court supports the fools from below and they are written upward

explanation.surface: A popular sentiment that the court is backing a bunch of idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upholds' does two jobs in a down entry: the fools are held up above CT, and they read upward. Nits is British slang for idiots.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the sense of a hunch: acting on a feeling means acting on gut sense rather than reason.

clue.text: One's onto Phil, outrageously to the right of Conservative old leader

indicators.note: one is on Phil, so the letter for one is attached to PHIL
an outrageous version is a wild one, so the letters of A and PHIL are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone is laying into a man called Phil, outrageously, to the right of a Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To the right of Conservative' sounds political, as if Phil is further right than the Tories; it only places letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the title belonged to the successors of Muhammad who led the early Islamic world, so an old leader.

clue.text: Prince puts on dress for a poke

indicators.note: to put on a dress is to get into it, but here the prince is put on top of the dress in a down entry

explanation.surface: A prince gets dressed up for a bit of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poke' has a racy surface meaning here; the definition is a prod.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym as nouns: a prod or exploratory jab, as with a surgeon's instrument.

clue.text: Bigwig shot semen (two rounds)

indicators.note: shot means wrecked, as in 'my nerves are shot', so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A crude Private Eye line about a big shot's bodily exploits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' pretends to be a verb of ejaculation; it is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiomatic noun use, as in 'she thinks she's really someone': a person of importance.

clue.text: A certain key girl's rather bourgeoise

parts.note: one particular piano key, the note nearest the middle of the keyboard

explanation.surface: A particular young woman is a bit bourgeois.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' is a piano key, not a musical key signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: bourgeois describes the property-owning middle ranks of society and their conventional tastes.

clue.text: As PM Boris and many of his cabinet produced nation on dole? No getting away from it

definitions.text: As PM Boris and many of his cabinet
definitions.note: the definition describes what Johnson and colleagues were; the answer works as an adjective here

indicators.note: to produce is to make something new out of material, so the letters are refashioned

explanation.surface: A sneer that Boris's cabinet put the country on benefits, and there's no escaping it.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the elite English boarding school; Boris Johnson and many of his ministers went there. 'No getting away from it' is the setter's aside, and the dole is British unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the clue lists people who share one background, and the answer names it.

clue.text: Sunak's first to abandon explosive study — respect!

indicators.note: an explosive mixture blows apart, so these letters are scattered and reassembled
the named letter leaves the mixture, so it is not used
first takes only the opening letter of Sunak's

parts.note: S is the opening letter of Sunak's

explanation.surface: A political jibe about Sunak dropping an explosive report and demanding respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explosive' shuffles STUDY, and S (Sunak's 'first' letter) is set 'to abandon' the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Duty can mean the respect or deference owed to someone, as in 'paying one's duty'.

clue.text: Pootle as Cyclops would, leading 'The Mexican U-turn'

indicators.note: to lead is to go in front, so the setter's contribution comes first

parts.note: the setter, talking of himself, would say 'I would', shortened

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came

explanation.surface: An odd headline: the setter would drift along, like a Mexican doing a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As Cyclops would' looks like part of the definition; it is the setter speaking as himself, I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym as verbs: to pootle is British for to potter along with no great purpose.

clue.text: Close attention, chaps: Times leader is just sweet talk

parts.note: to lend an ear is to pay attention

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A jibe that a Times editorial is all flattery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times leader' pretends to be the newspaper's editorial column; it is just its letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: an affectionate word or phrase like 'darling', the stuff of sweet talk.

clue.text: What the country's suffered under Sunak, Truss, Johnson and May initially — before useless Mr Gove sent in

definitions.text: What the country's suffered under Sunak, Truss, Johnson

indicators.note: before puts this letter ahead of the next piece
initially points to the opening letter of May

parts.note: M is the opening letter of May

indicators.note: useless letters are no good as they stand and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A satirical verdict on the run of recent Conservative prime ministers, with Michael Gove dragged in.
explanation.walkthrough: M (May 'initially') comes 'before' ISGOVERNMENT, which 'useless' makes from MR GOVE SENT IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Misgovernment is bad rule, which the clue claims the country has endured under these prime ministers.

clue.text: Herb's right to get stuck into ex-PM with a mace, though no expert

parts.note: an ace is an expert; removed from MACE

explanation.surface: A former prime minister is set upon by someone brandishing a mace, clumsily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' pretends to be a man's name; it is the definition. MACE without ACE leaves M, so 'a mace' gives AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a Mediterranean culinary herb related to oregano.

clue.text: Present unsatisfactory sort of reign

parts.note: off means below standard, as in food that has gone off

indicators.note: a sort of reign is a loose version of it, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dismissive comment on a monarch's lacklustre reign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges REIGN into ERING. 'Present' looks like the time but is a gift.
explanation.definitionFit: An offering is a gift, the same as a present.

clue.text: PM's working with the CIA — stressful

definitions.note: stressful here means full of stress, i.e. emphasis

indicators.note: working means in operation, and the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: The prime minister working with American intelligence is a stressful business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stressful' pretends to mean anxious; read it as full of stress, emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful literal reading: speech full of stress, in the sense of emphasis, is forceful.

clue.text: 'Time to join Ginsburg' — altogether not how Fox News would have presented it?

definitions.text: not how Fox News would have presented it

indicators.note: to join is to be attached

parts.note: Ruth Bader Ginsburg, US Supreme Court justice

explanation.surface: A news line about Ruth Bader Ginsburg's death, with a dig at how Fox would spin it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time to join Ginsburg' reads like a death notice; it only sets T beside her first name. Fox News is the right-leaning US channel.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by negation: a satirical dig that Fox's coverage would be anything but honest.

clue.text: Film star's signature "cheers"?

parts.note: a signature pairs an initial with a surname; this star's first name is Tom

explanation.surface: A fan asks whether an autograph is just a quick 'cheers'.
explanation.walkthrough: The star signs as initial plus surname, and the two run together into one ordinary word. Cheers is British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in British speech, where the drinking toast doubles as a casual thank-you.

clue.text: Conference venue sexual partner rolled up with a brief 18

indicators.note: in a down clue, rolled up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lay is slang for a sexual partner
18-down is THANKS, and TA is a brief, informal way of saying thanks

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of a conference venue where a lover is wrapped up with a quick thank-you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolled up' turns LAY into YAL; TA, a brief thank-you, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Yalta in Crimea hosted the 1945 conference of Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.

clue.text: Pope's terrible housing bother

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it inside, so the words hold the answer within them

explanation.surface: The Pope has terrible accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' pretends to be a noun, the Pope's lodgings; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym as nouns: a nuisance, something or someone that bothers you.

clue.text: Senior Whip outside Penny's shower

indicators.note: outside means surrounding

parts.note: S = senior, as in the abbreviation Sr

explanation.surface: A party's chief whip is waiting outside Penny's bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senior Whip' suggests a parliamentary whip; it is S plus LASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym as nouns: a spray or scattering of liquid.

clue.text: Balls on a course

parts.note: balls and rot both mean nonsense

explanation.surface: Golf balls out on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' reads as sports balls; it is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose sense: a set sequence or round of turns, a course followed in order.

clue.text: Problems post-Brexit may well not be, er, over, like this crossword?

definitions.text: Problems post-Brexit may well not be

indicators.note: over means turned around, so the word er is read backwards

parts.note: a crossword is meant to be solved, so it is solvable

explanation.surface: A wry aside that Brexit's problems may never be fixed, unlike this puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns ER into RE, which comes before SOLVABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something resolvable can be sorted out, which Brexit's problems may well never be.

clue.text: Book on masturbation? Not wife's job

explanation.surface: A cheeky query about a book on self-pleasure: not a job for the wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' reads as a chore for the wife; it is the definition. Without W the slang word becomes ANKING.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a line of work, the profession of bankers.

clue.text: Convenience of election-deniers assertions about a Democrat

parts.note: what election deniers assert are falsehoods

explanation.surface: Election deniers find it convenient to make claims about a Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convenience' pretends to be ease; a public convenience is a British public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A British euphemism: a public convenience is a toilet, and this is the women's one.
